catalog_quote: Phonological word shape: sesquisyllabic word structure in which presyllables are unstressed and somewhat reduced in form, consonant clusters on main syllables ... As in many Mon-Khmer languages, Kơho has two syllable types: a presyllable and a main syllable. The prototypical full phonological word (PW) takes a sesquisyllabic (‘syllable and a half’) form (Matisoff 1973:86). Thus, a word in Sre may be defined as consisting of a main syllable, optionally preceded by a presyllable (7). (7) PW = (presyllable) + Main syllable Metrically, such phonological words constitute an iambic construction of the type ( ̆ . --). ... Presyllables tend to weaken or disappear in many environments. ... Long vowels decrease in duration when they are not at the end of a word, particularly if unstressed. ... Generally speaking, duration decreases the further a syllable is from the final position in a word. For …

tone_statements.translation: 2. In Kơho, vowel length and pitch are two phonetic features that go together, but they manifest differently depending on the phonetic context, i.e. syllables with different endings. Phonologically, in syllables ending in consonants and glides one can distinguish long vowels - corresponding to low pitch - and short vowels - high pitch. 'Breathy' voice occurs only in syllables with low pitch and a long vowel. [...] The thesis chooses pitch as the phonologically relevant feature.

tone_statements.quote: Sự hình thành thanh điệu trong tiếng Mạ như đã nêu trên có thể gặp trong tiếng K’ho. Tiếng K’ho Srê (ở các huyện Di Linh và Bảo Lộc của Lâm Đồng) cũng là một ngôn ngữ có hai thanh cao và thấp, nhưng tiếng K’ho La Giạ ở huyện Hàm Thuận Bắc, tỉnh Bình Thuận mà chúng tôi có dịp khảo sát cũng đã có thanh “sắc”, “nặng”, “hỏi” trên cơ sở biến đổi của –q và –h.
tone_statements.translation: The formation of tone in Mạ as described above can also be met in K'ho. Srê K'ho (in Di Linh and Bảo Lộc districts of Lâm Đồng) is likewise a language with two tones, high and low, but the La Giạ K'ho of Hàm Thuận Bắc district, Bình Thuận province, which we had occasion to survey, already has 'sắc', 'nặng', 'hỏi' tones based on changes of -q and -h.

tone_statements.n_tones: K'ho Srê: 2 (high, low); K'ho La Giạ: 2 + sắc/nặng/hỏi-like contour tones

sources.note: Mạ, 'like K'ho', is a tone language with 2-5 tones by subdialect: northern Bảo Lộc varieties have two level tones, high vs low (low tone absent from open syllables and short-vowel syllables; both tones occur with voiced, voiceless and preglottalised onsets alike), Đạ Huoai/Đạ Tẻh varieties add sắc/nặng/hỏi-like contours compensating loss of final -q (glottal stop) and -h; high tone corresponds to Mnông short vowels, low tone to Mnông long vowels, so tonogenesis here runs through vowel length/finals, not onset devoicing. sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul J. 2000. Proto South Bahnaric: a reconstruction of a Mon-Khmer language of Indo-China. Pacific Linguistics 501. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, The Australian National University. 234 pp.
sources.note: States that South Bahnaric languages have not developed phonemic registers; Koho's normal vs falling 'tone' (after Manley 1972) is in complementary distribution with vowel length and therefore treated as non-distinctive; elsewhere uses a Koho 'falling tone' transcription in Ha Bul 1976 as evidence of a long vowel (etymon *hu:c comment). Secondhand for tone but an explicit analytic position.

tone.quote: Note that SB languages have not developed the phonemic registers found elsewhere in Mon-Khmer (such as Khmer or even some North Bahnaric languages). Koho is described by Manley (1972) as having a distinction between normal and falling tone, but this feature is in complementary distribution with vowel length, so it is not significant for this study.
